catalog_quote: A small number of words have no accented syllable of their own (certain conjunctions, most prepositions and the word ne 'not' before a verb are proclitics ...). Apart from these, every word form has one accented syllable (some compound words have one on each element). We say accent, not stress, because pitch and length are involved rather than intensity. Accent can alternate in placement or contour within the paradigm of a word. Accented syllables are termed either rising or falling, and contain a long or a short vowel. Traditional notation in grammars and dictionaries combines these two features, using four accent marks: short falling \\ as in ȁ, long falling ⌒ as in ȃ, short rising \ as in à, long rising ⁄ as in á. Read in full: Arsenijević & Simonović 2013 (lingbuzz preprint), Simonović & Kager 2023 (CC BY published form of the 2017 'From accent to stress' talk, via the Internet Archive), Diesing & Zec 2017 (Glossa, via the Internet Archive), Yu 2008 (UCLA MA, via the Internet Archive), plus two hrcak articles on Klaić 2013 (Opačić 2014, Vidović 2014) and the on-disk Zsiga & Zec 2013 / Zec & Zsiga 2010 / Landau et al. 1995. All first-hand statements agree with the catalog for the codified Neo-Štokavian standard: one contrastive lexical H (four traditional accents = tone x length), stress predictable from tone (initial, or the syllable before a non-initial H), falling accents only word-initial, no final accent in native words, monosyllables only falling. New refinement: Simonović & Kager 2023 document that the de facto standard in Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, Niš etc. is a stress-only system without tone or length (contrastive stress in nouns, predictable stem-final stress in verbs); Yu 2008 independently notes Zagreb speakers neutralise the pitch accent contrast. new_statements.quote: Standard Serbo-Croatian has two groups of varieties that differ in prosody. On the one hand, there are pitch-accent varieties with contrastive vowel length, spoken in what is traditionally considered the Neo-Štokavian dialect area (e.g., in Osijek, Zadar, Split, Novi Sad and Belgrade). On the other hand, there are stress varieties without contrastive vowel length, spoken in cities in what are traditionally considered Old-Štokavian and Non-Štokavian dialect areas (e.g., in Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, Niš, Zaječar and Bor). [...] In stress standard SC the stress position in verbs is predictable [...] verbal stress in stress standard SC is typically stem-final.

new_statements.reading: Two coexisting implementations of the standard: (a) the codified Neo-Štokavian pitch accent standard, in which a lexical high tone plus length is contrastive and stress is derived from tone (initial, or the syllable before a non-initial H; never final) — this is what the catalog codes as 'tonal' and what Zsiga & Zec 2013 (also read: 'stress falls on the syllable that immediately precedes the one specified for tone, if there is one, otherwise on the initial syllable.. stress cannot fall on the final syllable of polysyllables') describe; and (b) the urban 'stress standard' (Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, Niš, Bor, Zaječar), a pure lexical-stress system with no tone or length, contrastive stress in nouns (ˈnovine vs noˈvine) and predictable stem-final stress in verbs. So the catalog's 'tonal' coding is correct for the codified standard but this search of works with stress in the title documents a large stress-only variety of the same language that a lexical-stress catalog should note.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog's classification of the codified standard as tonal/pitch accent (High Tone plus stress; stress derived from tone) and with the Zsiga & Zec statement already held by the project; contributes no placement rule and nothing about the urban stress-only varieties.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Schütze treats Serbo-Croatian word prosody as a lexical High Tone (pitch accent) plus stress system, following Inkelas & Zec 1988 / Zec 1993: every prosodic word surfaces with a High Tone and stress (toneless words get a default High Tone), and tone spreading rules operate within words and, in some dialects, from a word onto a preceding preposition. He gives no rule for where stress or the accent falls within the word; the paper is about second-position clitics and uses accent only as a diagnostic for prosodic-word status.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect variation in tone spreading: in the Old Štokavian dialect (Zec 1993) High Tone spreads only from the final mora of a prosodic word, so an enclitic blocks spreading (dobro mi došli, p. 56); Neo-Štokavian spreads onto prepositions. The literature disagrees on whether function words such as the complementizer da are accented (Browne 1975, Magner 1991 yes; Progovac 1993, Radanović-Kocić 1988 no), and normally unaccented prepositions can carry emphatic or contrastive stress (p. 54).
new_statements.identity_note: Schütze 1994 writes about 'Serbo-Croatian' as the standard language, with side remarks on the Old Štokavian dialect (tone spreading only from a prosodic word's final mora) versus the Neo-Štokavian standard (spreading onto prepositions). Zlatić 1997 describes Serbian (Neo-Štokavian standard, with the four-way rising/falling long/short accents implicit in her 'short rising' vs 'long rising' examples). Neither describes the Zagreb or other urban stress-only varieties recorded in the existing Simonović & Kager statement.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tonal/pitch accent coding (Browne & Alt 2004: 'accent, not stress, because pitch and length are involved') and identical in content to the existing statement already held by the project for this entry: default = initial falling accent; adds the claim of a second post-lexical pattern (penult-final rising span) for lexicalised items. Says nothing about the tone-less urban 'stress standard' varieties (Simonović & Kager 2023 statement).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Neo-Štokavian Serbo-Croatian words carry lexical tonal accents; words without lexical tone get the default initial falling accent (initial stress + H); the authors argue for a second post-lexical (default) pattern, a rising accent spanning the last two syllables (stress on the penult, H on the final), found in lexicalised (non-paradigmatic) deverbal/deadjectival nominalisations and in a few idiomatic locative singulars of toneless inanimate nouns ('deaccentuation'), obligatory in nominalisations of perfective verbs, possible in deadjectival nouns with a toneless base and a long closed final syllable, lexically limited in plain nouns.
new_statements.exceptions: Deaccentuation to the final rising span is obligatory for deverbal nouns from perfective verbs; in deadjectival nominalisations only when the base is toneless and its final syllable long and closed; in underived nouns limited to a few toneless inanimate nouns in fixed locative expressions (na svakom korAAku 'everywhere' vs compositional na petom kOraaku).
new_statements.identity_note: Work 2 (and the leads) describe standard Neo-Štokavian Serbo-Croatian (the four-accent pitch accent standard of Serbia/Croatia/Bosnia); Simonović & Kager 2020 additionally contrasts it with the stress-only urban standard varieties (Zagreb, Rijeka, Niš etc.). Work 1 concerns loc.sg forms of toneless inanimate polysyllables in the same standard. Work 0 is about coordinating conjunctions (i, ili, ni, a, ali), not phonology.

tone_statements.quote: Croatian, along with the other Serbo-Croatian standard varieties, is most often characterized as a pitch accent language (Pletikos & Vlašić, 2007; Lehiste & Ivić, 1996). Traditionally, four types of accents are distinguished: short falling, short rising, long falling and long rising. ... (1.1) The four accents of Croatian Short falling: kȉša ‘rain’, stȁrac ‘old man’ Short rising: sèstra ‘sister’, kùpus ‘cabbage’ Long falling: pȋvo ‘beer’, dȏći ‘to come, inf.’ Long rising: ráditi ‘to do, inf.’, prózor ‘window’ Distinctive opposion of tone occurs only in words with an initial accented syllable
tone_statements.summary: pitch accent language with four accents (SF, SR, LF, LR) plus contrastive posttonal length; author's analysis (Hypothesis 1, p. 94, confirmed p. 210): two tonal categories, falling vs rising, quantity independent. TBU is the mora (p. 101). F0 production study, 10 speakers; only intonational downstep.

tone_statements.citation: Godjevac, Svetlana. 2000. An Autosegmental/Metrical Analysis of Serbo-Croatian Intonation. Ohio State University Working Papers in Linguistics 54: 79-142. hdl 1811/81027.
tone_statements.quote: Standard Serbo-Croatian (SC) is a lexical pitch-accent language. That is, words are specified not just for the location of stress, but also for the shape of the pitch accent that is aligned to the stressed syllable. All previous analyses (...) recognize four different types of pitch accents: short and long falling and short and long rising. ... The falling accents can be characterized as ... a sequence of a high (H) tone and a low (L) tone. The rising accents can be characterized as ... a L tone followed by a H tone. ... These accents are lexically contrastive, and hence, they are phonemic.
tone_statements.summary: Lexical pitch accent: traditional four accents reduced by the author to two bitonal ones, falling H*+L vs rising L*+H (length segmental), on a mora of the lexically stressed syllable; F0 study, 9 speakers. Only a post-lexical downtrend (downstepping of successive H) described; %L/%H boundary tones.

tone_statements.summary: Four traditional accents (short/long x falling/rising); Rehder reduces them to two features of the first syllable nucleus: pitch direction (rising vs falling) and quantity. Rising/falling contrast only in first syllable of polysyllables; intensity redundant. Acoustic plus perception tests.

sources.quote: A small number of words have no accented syllable of their own (certain conjunctions, most prepositions and the word ne 'not' before a verb are proclitics ...). Apart from these, every word form has one accented syllable (some compound words have one on each element). We say accent, not stress, because pitch and length are involved rather than intensity. Accent can alternate in placement or contour within the paradigm of a word. Accented syllables are termed either rising or falling, and contain a long or a short vowel. Traditional notation in grammars and dictionaries combines these two features, using four accent marks: short falling \\ as in ȁ, long falling ⌒ as in ȃ, short rising \ as in à, long rising ⁄ as in á. sources.quote: The rising accent is a tonal span over the accented syllable (which hosts the stress) and the syllable following it. [...] Whenever there is an underlying tone hosted by a non-initial syllable, it will create a rising span over the originally tone-bearing syllable and the one preceding it (hence vòda/vOdA) and the stress will be located on the left syllable of the span. This, in combination with the general ban on final stress explains why all non-initial accents are rising (at least in native words), so that a form like *vodA is excluded. sources.note: OUP chapter (paywalled) but the lingbuzz preprint is open. Restates the standard generative picture: lexical H tone is contrastive; stress is predictable from tone (on the syllable before a non-initial H, on the initial syllable otherwise); falling accents only word-initial; no final stress in native words; toneless words get a default initial falling accent. Main topic is -ost nominalisations, where the 'unmarked' pattern is a rising span over a long closed penult and the final syllable.

sources.quote: Serbian (srb) is a South Slavic (Indo-European) language with lexical pitch accent. [...] According to traditional accounts, Serbian has four accent types that contrast on stressed syllables (Lehiste & Ivić, 1986): short falling (e.g., lȕka 'onion.gen'); short rising (e.g., lùla 'smoking pipe'); long falling (e.g., Lûka 'Luka [name]); and long rising (e.g., lúka 'harbor'). All words in Serbian, excluding function words such as clitics and prepositions, have one primary stress, and thus one accent (Zec, 2005). [...] Rising accents can occur on any (non-final) syllable, but falling accents can only occur initially [...] In both dialects, the interactions between tones and segments were parallel in rising accents when considering the segments of the post-tonic syllable, rather than the tonic syllable, indicating that the post-tonic syllable is the TBU for the lexical H in rising accents in both dialects. [...] In this proposal, stress is one syllable to the left of a lexical H in rising accent words, and on the same syllable as the lexical H in falling accents.

sources.quote: Standard Serbo-Croatian (SC) is a lexical pitch-accent language. That is, words are specified not just for the location of stress, but also for the shape of the pitch accent that is aligned to the stressed syllable. All previous analyses (...) recognize four different types of pitch accents: short and long falling and short and long rising. ... The falling accents can be characterized as ... a sequence of a high (H) tone and a low (L) tone. The rising accents can be characterized as ... a L tone followed by a H tone. ... These accents are lexically contrastive, and hence, they are phonemic.
